messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

David, a 32-year-old tutor, presented for treatment six months after the resolution of a protracted stalking incident involving a former student's parent. The ordeal began with unnervingly persistent messages but escalated over several weeks. The woman, convinced David was reciprocating her feelings, began following him home from the library where he met his students. He remembers the low, guttural growl of her motorcycle engine, a sound that became synonymous with the feeling of being hunted. The confrontation that finally led to a restraining order was the most terrifying part; she cornered him in a parking garage, her voice eerily calm as she detailed his daily routines, her expression of anger terrifyingly controlled. She told him he was being selfish, that he owed her his attention. The quiet intensity of her rage was more chilling than any shouting could have been.

In the months since, David has found no peace. His sense of pervasive threat is constant, manifesting as a knot of tension in his stomach and a sleeplessness that leaves him exhausted and frayed. This persistent feeling of being unsafe has primed him to perceive danger everywhere. Now, when walking home from a tutoring session, the sound of any motorcycle, no matter how distant, sends a jolt of adrenaline through him, and he is certain he is being followed again. His body reacts before his mind can catch up; his heart hammers against his ribs, and he ducks into a doorway, scanning the street for a threat that isn't there. This heightened state of alert means he is constantly misinterpreting benign cues as signs of danger, turning his daily commute into a series of false alarms.

These triggered moments do more than just frighten him; they serve as powerful confirmation of the new, terrifying beliefs he has formed about the world. When a parent expresses even mild frustration about their child's grades, the calm anger in their voice instantly transports him back to the garage. This experience reinforces his conviction that people are not what they seem, that a placid surface can hide a dangerous obsession. Each time he feels that jolt of fear, it solidifies his self-doubt; he thinks, "I should have seen it coming with her. I can't trust my own judgment about people." This core belief that he is unable to do the right thing or accurately read others has, in turn, made him exquisitely sensitive to potential threats, constantly scanning faces and listening to tones of voice, which only makes him more likely to encounter triggers.

This deeply ingrained mistrust has poisoned his life from the inside out. Convinced he is fundamentally broken and cannot trust his own instincts, David has begun to retreat from the world. He tells himself he deserves to suffer for his failure to protect himself, a thought that cycles through his mind as a form of quiet punishment. This belief that he is untrustworthy and that others are deceptive has made him pull away from his wife. He avoids being emotionally close with her, deflecting her questions and turning away from her touch. He cannot allow himself to relax, viewing it as a dangerous lapse in vigilance. He spends his evenings ostensibly watching television but is really listening for sounds outside, unable to settle.

His attempts to manage the fear only make it worse. By avoiding intimacy, he denies himself comfort and connection, leaving him isolated with his anxiety. The self-punishing thoughts and the refusal to ever let his guard down keep his nervous system in a constant state of high alert, which directly fuels his sense of ambient threat. His world has shrunk as a result; he now insists on tutoring students only at the public library, a familiar place, turning down new clients if it would require him to go to an unfamiliar home. The resulting loss of income has become another source of marital stress. David finally sought therapy after his wife, tearfully telling him she felt like she was living with a ghost, asked if he still wanted to be married. He is terrified of losing her, but even more terrified of the idea that he is right—that he is permanently broken and can no longer be trusted to keep himself, or anyone he loves, safe.
